title: The massacre of Vassy
shortBlurb: Troops of the Duke of Guise fell upon a Huguenot congregation at worship in Champagne, and the bloodshed opened France's Wars of Religion…
body: In January 1562 the regent Catherine de' Medici, seeking to hold France together, granted the Huguenots a measure of toleration by the Edict of Saint-Germain, permitting their worship outside the walled towns. Passing through Champagne on 1 March 1562, Francis, second Duke of Guise, came upon six or seven hundred Reformed Christians singing psalms in a barn at Vassy, within the town's liberties and so beyond the edict's leave.

Words were exchanged, stones flew, and the duke's men fired and charged; when the melee ended twenty-three worshippers lay dead and more than a hundred wounded — so the Catholic Encyclopedia's account, while Huguenot writers reckoned the slain far higher and named the deed a massacre.

The news raced through France. Condé and Coligny took up arms, seizing Orléans within the month, and Guise's party answered in kind: the first of the eight Wars of Religion had begun, a struggle that would burn for more than thirty years, through St. Bartholomew's Day and the League, until the Edict of Nantes closed it in 1598.

title: The election of Pope Pius XII
shortBlurb: On his sixty-third birthday Eugenio Pacelli was chosen pope in the swiftest conclave of modern times, on the eve of world war…
body: Pius XI died on 10 February 1939, and the conclave that assembled on 1 March proved the shortest of modern times. On the second day, 2 March, the cardinals chose Eugenio Pacelli on the third ballot — his sixty-third birthday — and he took the name Pius XII. He was the first cardinal Secretary of State to be elected pope since Clement IX in 1667.

Born in Rome on 2 March 1876 and ordained in 1899, Pacelli had spent his priesthood in the Holy See's diplomacy: nuncio in Munich and Berlin through the First World War and the Weimar years, cardinal in 1929, then Secretary of State, negotiating the 1933 Concordat with the German Reich and sharing in the drafting of Pius XI's protest Mit brennender Sorge.

His election was the first announced to the world by radio. Crowned on 12 March, he guided the Church through the Second World War and the age of communism that followed, defining the dogma of the Assumption in 1950, before dying at Castel Gandolfo on 9 October 1958.

title: The election of Pope Eugene IV
shortBlurb: A Venetian nephew of Gregory XII was chosen pope in the first conclave after the Great Schism, and his stormy reign saw union proclaimed with the Greeks…
body: Martin V died on 20 February 1431, and in the first conclave held since the healing of the Great Schism the cardinals chose, on 3 March 1431 — or on the fourth, as some older authorities reckon — Gabriele Condulmer of Venice, a nephew of Gregory XII made cardinal in 1408. Crowned on 11 March, he took the name Eugene IV.

His long pontificate was a running battle with the conciliar movement: he dissolved the Council of Basel at its opening in 1431, was driven from Rome into exile at Florence in 1434, and fought for years to recover his city. Yet it was Eugene who presided over the Council of Ferrara and Florence, where on 6 July 1439 the decree Laetentur Caeli proclaimed union with the Greeks.

In Florence he also consecrated, on 25 March 1436, the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore beneath Brunelleschi's new dome. Restored to Rome in 1443, he died there on 23 February 1447, having held the papacy through some of its most turbulent years.

title: The birth of Prince Henry the Navigator
shortBlurb: The Portuguese prince who sent his captains ever southward down the African coast was born at Porto, and the age of discovery had begun…
body: Henry, called the Navigator, was born at Porto on 4 March 1394, a younger son of King John I of Portugal and Philippa of Lancaster. At twenty-one he fought at the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, and from 1420 he was governor of the Order of Christ, turning its revenues to the work that filled his life: the exploration of the African coast.

Year by year his captains felt their way south — rediscovering Porto Santo in 1418 and Madeira in 1420 and settling them, passing the dreaded Cape Bojador under Gil Eanes in 1434, and reaching the Senegal and the Gambia in the 1440s. The voyages sought gold and allies against Islam — the fabled Prester John — and carried the Cross to unbaptized peoples.

Later tradition has made his retreat at Sagres a school of navigation, though historians doubt its formal existence. Henry died there on 13 November 1460; within two generations the path he opened had carried Dias to the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and da Gama to India in 1498.

title: The Third Lateran Council
shortBlurb: Alexander III gathered the Church at the Lateran to repair the schism — and fixed the two-thirds rule by which popes are chosen still…
body: Fresh from the Peace of Venice, which in 1177 had ended his eighteen-year schism with Frederick Barbarossa and a line of antipopes, Alexander III summoned the Church to the Lateran. The council opened on 5 March 1179, as Archbishop William of Tyre, our chief witness, records, with some three hundred bishops and a great body of abbots gathered about the pope.

In three sessions the fathers issued twenty-seven canons. The first reserved papal elections to the cardinals alone and required a two-thirds majority — the rule by which conclaves have been governed ever since. Others condemned the Cathar heretics of southern France and the mercenary bands then ravaging Christendom, forbade Jews and Muslims to keep Christian servants, and charged every cathedral church to maintain a schoolmaster for poor scholars.

Reckoned the eleventh ecumenical council, the Third Lateran repaired the wreckage of the schism and set the legal frame of the medieval papacy on firmer ground; thirty-six years later Innocent III would build upon it at the Fourth.

title: The death of Pope Celestine II
shortBlurb: A gentle scholar who had studied under Abelard, he reigned only five months and lifted the interdict from France…
body: Guido di Castello had sat at the feet of Peter Abelard and kept his friendship even after the master's condemnation at Sens in 1140. Made cardinal-deacon by Honorius II in 1127 and cardinal-priest of San Marco by Innocent II, whom he had served as legate in France, he was chosen pope on 26 September 1143 and consecrated on 3 October.

His brief reign was merciful: one of his first acts lifted the interdict Innocent II had laid upon France in the quarrel over the archbishopric of Bourges, restoring King Louis VII to the Church's peace. A harder contest, over the legatine rights claimed by King Roger II of Sicily, he left unsettled.

After five months and thirteen days Celestine died at Rome on 8 March 1144, at the Palladium monastery on the Palatine — of the plague then wasting Italy, says the old account — and was buried at the Lateran. His short pontificate closed quietly, while in France his old master Abelard's troubles were ending at Cluny.

title: The election of Pope Leo X
shortBlurb: A Medici deacon of thirty-seven became pope — patron of Raphael's Rome, and the pope who excommunicated Martin Luther…
body: Julius II died on 21 February 1513, and the conclave that followed chose, on 9 March, Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, second son of Lorenzo the Magnificent; proclaimed two days later, he took the name Leo X. Made a cardinal at thirteen, he had been only a deacon: he was ordained priest on 15 March, consecrated bishop on the seventeenth, and crowned on the nineteenth — the last man not yet a priest to be elected pope.

His eight years were golden and ruinous together: the Rome of Raphael and the rising St. Peter's, and the preaching of indulgences to pay for it, which moved Martin Luther to post his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517. Leo answered with Exsurge Domine in 1520, condemning forty-one propositions, and with the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem of 3 January 1521, which excommunicated Luther.
He died on 1 December 1521, aged forty-five, leaving the papal treasury deep in debt and Christendom on the edge of its great division.

title: The martyrdom of St. John Ogilvie
shortBlurb: Scotland's only post-Reformation martyr was hanged at Glasgow Cross for refusing the king's supremacy over the Church…
body: Born about 1580 at Drumnakeith in Banffshire and raised a Calvinist, John Ogilvie was received into the Church at Louvain in 1597 and entered the Society of Jesus two years later. Ordained at Paris in 1613, he begged for the Scottish mission and returned home that November, disguised as a horse trader, to minister in secret about Glasgow.

His mission lasted less than a year. Arrested in October 1614, he was tortured by sleeplessness and pressed to own King James's supremacy in the Church, which he refused — he would acknowledge it, he said, no more than that of an old hat. Condemned for treason, he was hanged at Glasgow Cross on 10 March 1615, throwing his hidden rosary into the crowd as he died.

Out of open popular sympathy the customary quartering was spared him. Beatified in 1929, he was canonized by Paul VI on 17 October 1976 — the only post-Reformation martyr of Scotland raised to the altars.

title: The Triumph of Orthodoxy
shortBlurb: On the first Sunday of Lent in 843, after a century of iconoclasm, the holy icons came home to Hagia Sophia in triumph…
body: Twice the Church of the East had cast out the holy icons, and twice the images came home. After the Second Council of Nicaea restored them in 787, iconoclasm rose again under Leo the Armenian and the Emperor Theophilus; but at Theophilus's death his widow Theodora ruled for the child Michael III, and with Patriarch Methodios she summoned a synod at Constantinople to make peace.

On the first Sunday of Lent, 11 March 843, the whole city walked in triumph from the church of Blachernae to Hagia Sophia, and the icons were set again in their places. The synod decreed that the anniversary should be kept each year on that same Sunday — the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

With that procession a struggle of more than a century ended: no emperor ever again moved against the images. To this day the first Sunday of Great Lent keeps the victory in every church of the Byzantine rite, where the Synodikon is still read with its cries of 'Eternal Memory' for the confessors and its anathemas for the heresiarchs.

title: The encyclical Mit brennender Sorge
shortBlurb: Smuggled into the Reich and read from every Catholic pulpit on Palm Sunday, Pius XI's encyclical dared to indict the Nazi creed…
body: In the first months of 1937 the German bishops begged Pius XI for a word that could not be silenced. The answer was written in German, not Latin, with the hand of Cardinal Secretary Pacelli and of Cardinal Faulhaber of Munich in its drafting, and dated Passion Sunday, 14 March 1937: the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, 'on the situation of the Catholic Church in the German Reich'.

Copies were smuggled across the border and secretly reproduced — some three hundred thousand, pressed and typed by hand — so that on Palm Sunday, 21 March, the letter was read entire from the pulpits of every Catholic church in Germany before the Gestapo could seize a copy.

It named neither Hitler nor his party, yet it catalogued the regime's breaches of the 1933 Concordat, condemned the distortion and denial of the Christian faith, and warned against the idolatrous exaltation of race and people. Reprisals against clergy and Catholic schools sharpened in answer. Five days later, on 19 March, Pius signed its companion, Divini Redemptoris, against atheistic communism.

sources.text: Mit brennender Sorge, Pius XI, 14 March 1937 (vatican.va)

title: The conclave of Venice elects Pope Pius VII
shortBlurb: With Rome in French hands and Pius VI dead in captivity, the cardinals elected a Benedictine at Venice in the last conclave held outside Rome…
body: Pius VI died on 29 August 1799, a prisoner of the French Directory at Valence, with Rome in French hands and the papal treasures scattered. The cardinals gathered where they could: at the Benedictine abbey of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, under Austrian protection, opening their conclave on 30 November 1799 — the last conclave ever held outside Rome.

Deadlocked for three and a half months, the thirty-five electors at last united on 14 March 1800 upon Barnaba Chiaramonti, the Benedictine bishop of Imola, who took the name Pius VII. Crowned on 21 March with a makeshift tiara, he reached Rome in July.

His twenty-three years remade the Church in the new Europe: the Concordat of 1801 with Bonaparte, the coronation of Napoleon at Notre-Dame in 1804, then arrest in 1809 and five years of captivity at Savona and Fontainebleau, the return in 1814, and the restoration of the Society of Jesus by Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum on 7 August of that year. He died on 20 August 1823.

title: Columbus returns in triumph to Palos
shortBlurb: Two hundred and twenty-four days after sailing for the Indies, Columbus anchored the Niña again at Palos, and Europe learned of a new world…
body: They had sailed from Palos on 3 August 1492, after Mass, in the Santa María, the Pinta, and the Niña; on 12 October they made landfall at an island its people called Guanahani, which Columbus christened San Salvador. When the Santa María was wrecked at Christmas, he left thirty-nine men at La Navidad and turned home with the two caravels.

The return nearly killed them: a February storm parted the little ships, and Columbus sealed an account of his discovery in a barrel against the worst. The Niña reached the Tagus on 4 March 1493 and at last, on 15 March, dropped anchor again at Palos — a few hours only before the tardy Pinta — two hundred and twenty-four days after sailing.

His letter to the treasurer Santángel, printed within weeks, told Europe of a new world. On his second voyage, that September, seventeen ships carried twelve hundred men — and with Fray Buil and Fray Ramón Pane, the first missionaries — beginning the evangelization of the Americas.

title: Magellan sights the Philippines
shortBlurb: After ninety-nine days of empty ocean, Magellan's fleet raised the island of Samar, and the Gospel's road to the Philippines began…
body: Five ships under Ferdinand Magellan had cleared the strait that bears his name in November 1520 and crossed ninety-nine days of empty ocean, past the Ladrones, when at daybreak on 16 March 1521 the lookout raised a high land — the island of Zamal, which we call Samar. So Antonio Pigafetta, the expedition's chronicler, records it.

Magellan named the archipelago the Isles of St. Lazarus, watered at Homonhon, and on Easter Sunday, 31 March, his chaplain Pedro de Valderrama offered the first Mass in the Philippines at Mazaua. At Cebu the rajah Humabon and hundreds of his people received baptism in April — the seed of the faith in Asia's great Catholic nation.

Magellan himself fell at Mactan on 27 April 1521, but his Victoria sailed on under Elcano to complete the first circumnavigation in September 1522. Within fifty years Legazpi and the friars had planted the Church in the islands for good.

title: The martyrdom of St. Gabriel Lalemant
shortBlurb: The young Jesuit who had begged for the hardest mission bore the fire through a long night in Huronia, one of the North American Martyrs…
body: Gabriel Lalemant, born at Paris in 1610, entered the Jesuits at twenty and spent years pleading for the hardest mission; he reached Canada only in 1646. Three years later the Iroquois war came down upon Huronia: on 16 March 1649 a war band overran the mission of St. Louis and seized Fathers Jean de Brébeuf and Lalemant.

Carried to St. Ignace, Brébeuf bore the fire for a few hours and died that same day. The tormentors kept Lalemant longer: burned from evening through the night — seared with hatchets, his eyes put out, boiling water poured over him in mockery of baptism — he died on the morning of 17 March 1649.

The mission of Sainte-Marie was abandoned and burned, and the Huron nation scattered to the winds. Lalemant, Brébeuf, and their six companions — the North American Martyrs — were canonized together by Pius XI on 29 June 1930; their feast is kept on 19 October.

title: The last imperial coronation in Rome
shortBlurb: Nicholas V crowned Frederick III of Habsburg emperor in St. Peter's — the last imperial coronation the city of Rome would ever see…
body: Frederick III of Habsburg, elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt in 1440, came down into Italy in the first weeks of 1452 for a bride and a crown. Meeting Eleanor of Portugal at Siena, he entered Rome with her on 9 March; Pope Nicholas V joined them in marriage on the sixteenth.

Three days later, on 19 March 1452, the feast of St. Joseph, Nicholas crowned Frederick emperor in St. Peter's. It was the last imperial coronation Rome would ever see: after Frederick only Charles V, in 1530 at Bologna, received the imperial crown from a pope's hands, and no emperor again from within the city.

His coronation opened the Habsburg tenure of the empire that endured, with a single gap, until Francis II laid the title down in 1806; the Concordat of Vienna of 1448, made in the same understanding, governed the Church in the German lands for nearly as long. Frederick reigned fifty-three years, the longest of any emperor.

title: The death of Ebbo of Reims
shortBlurb: The archbishop of Reims who presided over the public penance of Louis the Pious, and was twice deposed in the Carolingian civil wars, died in retirement…
body: Born a serf on the royal fisc and raised at the palace school, Ebbo became librarian to Louis the Pious and, in 816, archbishop of Reims. In 822 at Attigny he presided over the emperor's public penance for the blinding and death of his nephew Bernard of Italy — a spectacle of imperial humility the age never forgot.

He preached the Gospel among the Danes in the years that prepared St. Ansgar's mission; but in the wars of Louis's sons he chose Lothair's side, and at Soissons in 833 he led the bishops who deposed the emperor and imposed a second public penance. Louis's restoration brought Ebbo's fall: imprisoned, he was deposed at Thionville in 835 and shut up at Fulda.

Restored to Reims by Lothair in 840, he was driven out for good after Fontenoy and died in retirement on 20 March 851. The school of manuscript painting he fostered at Reims left him a memorial in the radiant Ebbo Gospels, which still bears his name.

title: The suppression of the Knights Templar
shortBlurb: In a secret consistory at Vienne, Clement V dissolved the Order of the Temple 'by way of provision', and the Templars were no more…
body: The blow had fallen in a single dawn: on Friday, 13 October 1307, every Templar in France was seized at King Philip's command, and confessions of blasphemy and heresy were wrung from many by torture. Clement V, after years of inquiry, summoned the Council of Vienne in October 1311 to judge the Order.

The fathers leaned toward hearing the Templars' defense, but the king descended on Vienne in person. On the Wednesday of Holy Week, 22 March 1312, in a secret consistory, Clement suppressed the Order — not by definitive sentence upon its guilt, but 'by way of provision', as the bull Vox in excelso declares, published in the council's second session on 3 April.

By Ad providam of 2 May the Templars' goods passed chiefly to the Hospitallers; the last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, held a prisoner, was burned at Paris on 19 March 1314. The Chinon parchment, found in the Vatican archives, records that the pope had absolved the Order's leaders — the suppression stood as policy, not as judgment.

title: The death of Pope Julius III
shortBlurb: The cardinal who had opened the Council of Trent became its restorer as pope, and died as England returned to Rome…
body: Giovanni Maria del Monte had stood at the Council of Trent's cradle: made a cardinal by Paul III in 1536, he was first of the three legates who opened the council on 13 December 1545. Elected pope on 7 February 1550 after ten weeks of conclave, against the emperor's wishes, he took the name Julius III.

He kept the jubilee of 1550, confirmed the young Society of Jesus by Exposcit debitum, and founded the Collegium Germanicum in 1552 to form priests for the embattled German Church. At the emperor's urging he called the fathers back to Trent in May 1551, where they defined the doctrine of the Eucharist, penance, and anointing — until war scattered them again within a year.

His eyes reached also to England: when Mary Tudor came to the throne he sent Cardinal Pole home as legate, and in November 1554 the realm was reconciled to Rome. Worn by gout, Julius died at Rome on 23 March 1555; his Villa Giulia still witnesses the gentler side of his reign.

title: The coronation of Conrad II
shortBlurb: On Easter Sunday 1027, John XIX crowned Conrad II emperor in Old St. Peter's, with Cnut and the king of Burgundy looking on…
body: The Salian century began with a crown: Conrad, first of his line, elected king in September 1024 when Henry II died childless, came down into Italy in 1026, took the Iron Crown of the Lombards at Milan, and reached Rome for Easter.

On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1027, Pope John XIX crowned him emperor in Old St. Peter's, and his queen Gisela empress. Kings stood about the altar — Cnut of England and Denmark, then a pilgrim in Rome, and Rudolph III of Burgundy — with some seventy prelates, the archbishops of Cologne, Mainz, Trier, Magdeburg, Salzburg, Milan, and Ravenna; the solemnities lasted seven days, troubled by a precedence quarrel between Milan and Ravenna that Conrad settled for Milan.

So began the Salian emperors — Conrad II, Henry III, Henry IV, Henry V — whose hundred years carried both the Church's reform and the investiture struggle. Cnut wrote home to his English people of the honor shown him there, a letter that survives.

title: The encyclical Populorum progressio
shortBlurb: Paul VI's Easter encyclical summoned the rich nations to the service of the poor, declaring that development is the new name for peace…
body: On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1967, Paul VI signed the encyclical Populorum progressio, 'on the development of peoples' — the fruit of his journeys to India and to the United Nations, and of the Council's teaching in Gaudium et spes.

The letter took the world's measure: a gulf widening between rich nations and poor, commerce that rewarded the strong, and peoples whose hunger for bread was also a hunger for dignity. 'Development', the pope declared, 'is the new name for peace' — and he asked the wealthy nations for aid without domination, fair prices for poor countries' goods, and a world fund fed from what the rich count superfluous.

John Paul II marked its twentieth year with Sollicitudo rei socialis in 1987, and the Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace was established in its wake. Its principle — that the Church owes service to the whole human family and not to souls alone — has framed every later social encyclical, down to Caritas in veritate in 2009.

title: The death of Pope Stephen IX
shortBlurb: The legate of Hagia Sophia in 1054 and a reforming pope of eight months, he died at Florence while the factions plotted his succession…
body: Frederick of Lorraine, brother of Duke Godfrey the Bearded, had been archdeacon at Liège when Leo IX drew him to Rome and made him chancellor. In 1054 he stood with the two other legates who laid the bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius upon the altar of Hagia Sophia — the act remembered as the opening of the East–West schism.

Made abbot of Monte Cassino and cardinal by Victor II, he was chosen pope at the beginning of August 1057, five days after Victor's death, and took the name Stephen IX. His eight months pressed the reform of the clergy against simony and unlawful marriage, while with his brother he planned to drive the Normans from the south.

Setting out toward Tuscany, he died at Florence on 29 March 1058, having first forbidden the Romans, under pain of his curse, to elect a successor before Hildebrand's return from Germany. The Tusculan nobles ignored him and crowned Benedict X within days — and Hildebrand's party answered with Nicholas II, in whose reign papal elections passed to the cardinals.

title: The Sicilian Vespers
shortBlurb: A quarrel at the church of the Holy Spirit on Easter Monday set Sicily ablaze and broke the Angevin empire of the Mediterranean…
body: Charles of Anjou, the papacy's champion, had taken the Hohenstaufen kingdom of the Two Sicilies at Benevento and Tagliacozzo, and his French officials ruled it harshly. On Easter Monday, 30 March 1282 — some older accounts say the Tuesday — at the hour of vespers, a quarrel outside Palermo's church of the Holy Spirit, where tradition says a French sergeant insulted a Sicilian bride, set the city alight.

'Death to the French!' ran through Palermo, and through the island: for six weeks the rising hunted the Angevins down — thousands perished, and suspects were tried by the word ciciri, which French tongues could not pronounce.

The Sicilians called in Peter III of Aragon, who landed at Trapani that summer; Pope Martin IV excommunicated him and preached a crusade for Aragon, but the Angevin cause was broken. The War of the Vespers burned on to the Peace of Caltabellotta in 1302, which parted Sicily to Aragon from Naples to Anjou — and Charles's dream of a Mediterranean empire died at Palermo.
